newsitem.title: INDIA: India regulator pledges carry-forward trade panel.
newsitem.headline: India regulator pledges carry-forward trade panel.

text.p: India's stockmarket watchdog on Wednesday pledged to set up a committee to review the carry-forward system of share trading, currently allowed only under strict conditions.

Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) chairman D.R. Mehta also said the regulator had decided on a uniform lock-in period of three years for promoters' contributions to equity. Currently, the lock-in period varies from two to five years.
"It has been decided by the board today to constitute a review group to examine various aspects of the carry-forward system," Mehta told a news conference.

Under carry-forward trading brokers can buy stocks by paying a nominal interest charge without actually taking delivery of the shares. The system also enables brokers to put off paying for their shares by paying only a fraction of the actual cost until the end of the particular trading cycle.

The committee, to be headed by SEBI member J.R. Verma, will include representatives from the Bombay Stock Exchange, the National Stock Exchange, the Unit Trust of India and an investors' association, Mehta said.

SEBI banned "badla" or carry forward trade in March 1994 on the grounds it was leading to excessive speculation. It introduced a modified system of carry-forward trade last year with several checks and balances but many brokers are keen to revive "badla" in its original form.
Mehta said in January that the brokers' demand was a "controversial issue" that needed to be studied.
Most shares on the Bombay and Delhi bourses ended lower ahead of the board meeting. The decision on carry-forward trading was announced only after the markets closed.
An advisory committee set up by SEBI said earlier this month that the lock-in period for promoters' contributions needed to be reduced to three years from five.

"The board felt that the period of three years should be uniformly applied for promoters' contribution for all public issues (of shares), and for rights issues there should be no promoters' contribution subjected to lock-in," Mehta said on Wednesday.

The lock-in period refers to a time period during which shares bought by promoters cannot be sold in the market. At present, the lock-in period for shares sold in new public issues ranges from two to five years.
For rights issues made at par there is currently no lock-in period, but there is one for rights shares issued at a premium.

The board also said it had decided to permit promoters of non-underwritten issues to mobilise funds within 60 days of the issue's closure, provided they have made adequate disclosures in the offer document. Only underwritten issues are currently allowed this facility. -- New Delhi newsroom +91 11 301 4654
